# Mahāgosiṅga Sutta (MN 32 (PTS MN i 212))

**ID:** MN 32 (PTS MN i 212)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Mahāgosiṅga Sutta  
**PTS:** MN i 212  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul3.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul3.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāgosiṅga Sutta* (MN 32) is set on a clear moonlit night in the Gosiṅga sāla-tree grove, where several eminent disciples gather [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. Sāriputta asks each elder in turn what type of practitioner would illuminate and adorn the forest [Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. The disciples provide answers reflecting distinct spiritual ideals: Ānanda praises the monk who has heard much and can teach all audiences effectively, while Mahāmoggallāna describes two monks engaging in doctrinal discussion (*abhidhammakathā*) who question each other without faltering [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Anderson 1999]. When the elders relate their exchange to the Buddha, he endorses all their responses as well spoken, but adds his own ideal: a monastic who enters meditation with the resolute determination not to break posture until all mental defilements are fully eradicated [Anālayo 2017; Buswell & Lopez 2014].

The sutta's mention of *abhidhammakathā* is prominent in Buddhist exegetical and modern scholarship. Buddhaghosa cites the text in his commentary to the *Abhidhamma Piṭaka* as scriptural authority that mastery of Abhidhamma enables monks to resolve doctrinal questions correctly [Anderson 1999; Anderson 2013]. Scholars observe that in this early discourse, *abhidhamma* functions alongside *dhammakathā*, signifying discussion "about" or "concerning" the Dhamma rather than a reference to a finalized Abhidhamma collection [Anālayo, Dawn of Abhidharma; Klaus & Hartmann 2007].

- [Klaus & Hartmann 2007] Bhikkhu Anālayo, in Konrad Klaus and Jens-Uwe Hartmann (eds.), Indica et Tibetica: Festschrift für Michael Hahn (2007) — Comparative analysis of speaker attributions across Pali, Sanskrit fragments, and Chinese parallels.
